data.title: Does the larger rapamycin benefit in female mice survive equal drug exposure, and is it set by hormones or by chromosomes?
data.gap: Emerged directly from the full-text effect sizes: S6K1-KO +19% median lifespan in FEMALES / no effect in males (SEL2009); rapamycin favors females (MIL2014 all doses in F vs top-2 in M; HAR2009 +38% F vs +28% M; FOK2014 +16% F vs +11% M), and so, more narrowly, does a genetic mTOR hypomorph (WUX2013 +22% F/+19% M); yet acarbose favors MALES (+22% vs +5%, HAR2014). Sex changes not just the magnitude but sometimes the DIRECTION of the response. BIT2016 needs a qualifier: its male-benefit / female-harm result holds only for the high-dose 8 mg/kg/day injection arm. In the same paper's 126 ppm dietary arm, post-treatment survival rose significantly in both sexes and a Cox model found no evidence that sex modified the treatment effect (p=0.904). BIT2016 therefore supports DOSE-dependent dimorphism, not intrinsic dimorphism, and is as much a boundary case for this hypothesis as evidence for it. The thesis stands on SEL2009, MIL2014, HAR2009, FOK2014, WUX2013 and HAR2014.
data.gap_beginner: Male and female animals often respond differently to these drugs – sometimes just by how much, but sometimes the effect flips direction entirely. Rapamycin tends to help females somewhat more; a different drug, acarbose, helps males more. Females also build up higher drug levels in their blood after the same dose, which may explain part of it.
data.changed_since_written: The endocrine half of this question is the better supported half, but the pharmacokinetic half was misdescribed here until 2026-10-10 and the correction matters. Exposure WAS measured. Miller 2014 (MIL2014, PMID 24341993, full text PMC4032600) quantified whole-blood rapamycin by HPLC-tandem mass spectrometry: females reached 7, 16 and 80 ng/mL at 4.7, 14 and 42 ppm against 6, 9 and 23 ng/mL in males, with a two-factor ANOVA giving sex p=0.007, dose p=0.003 and interaction p=0.03; a second cohort at 26 months showed higher female levels at every time point sampled. So the sex difference in drug exposure is an established measurement, not a speculation. What has NOT been tested is the causal step: whether equalising exposure abolishes the female advantage in lifespan. One observation inside the same paper (MIL2014, PMID 24341993) already argues against a purely pharmacokinetic account. At the lowest dose the exposures are close to equal (7 ng/mL in females against 6 in males), and the lifespan difference persists anyway: median lifespan +16% in females (p<0.0001) against +3% in males (p=0.19). If exposure were the whole explanation, that dose should have produced the smallest sex gap, not a large one. Note the design limit: those concentrations were measured in a separate set of animals from the survival cohort, so this is a weak version of the exposure-matched test rather than the real thing. The endocrine evidence is separate and stronger. Gonadectomy flips drug responses in both directions, castrated males losing most responses and ovariectomised females gaining male-like ones (Garratt, Aging Cell 2017, PMID 28834262); 17-alpha-estradiol improves sarcopenia in intact but not castrated males at the same dose and exposure (Garratt, Aging Cell 2019, PMID 30740872); and it engages the pathway in males only, whereas rapamycin and acarbose do so in both sexes (Shen, Aging Cell 2021, PMID 33742521). Newer work adds something the card did not anticipate: the direction flips by endpoint, not only by drug. Rapamycin favours females for lifespan and motor decline (Singh, J Gerontol A 2026, PMID 41863332), acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol favour males for lifespan - yet all three favour females for trabecular bone (Dall'Ara, bioRxiv 2026, preprint, not peer reviewed). One further piece suggests the female bias is not specific to mTOR drugs at all: female mice accumulate substantially more p16-positive cells than males across tissues, and in the p16-3MR model their ablation improved grip strength, skin regeneration and liver damage in females only (Lin, Adv Sci 2025, PMID 41168880). A dimorphism of the same direction in an intervention with no mTOR involvement weakens any purely pharmacokinetic account of the rapamycin gap.
data.still_open: Two narrow questions, neither of which is pharmacokinetics against pharmacodynamics - the exposure difference is measured, so only its causal weight is at issue. First: does the female advantage in rapamycin lifespan survive titrating both sexes to equal whole-blood trough concentrations? No study in this corpus has run that experiment deliberately, and it is the most directly falsifiable form of the PK claim. A weak version already exists inside MIL2014 and points away from PK: at 4.7 ppm the two sexes sit at 7 and 6 ng/mL and the gap is still +16% against +3%. That is suggestive, not decisive, because it is one dose in one cohort and exposure was measured in separate animals from the survival cohort. Second: is the governing variable gonadal hormone milieu rather than chromosomal sex? The claim that exposure-matching would narrow the gap for rapamycin but not for acarbose is untested in either direction and should not be read as established.
data.hypothesis: The governing variable is gonadal hormone milieu rather than chromosomal sex, and which sex benefits depends on the endpoint measured as well as on the drug.
data.hypothesis_beginner: Educated guess: what decides the difference is not being male or female as such, but which sex hormones are circulating — and the answer can flip depending on whether you measure lifespan, bone or movement.
data.how_to_test: Two experiments. First the deliberate exposure-matching study: titrate males and females to equal whole-blood rapamycin trough concentrations, confirmed in the survival animals themselves rather than in a separate pharmacokinetic cohort, and re-measure lifespan. Powering matters here - MIL2014's own near-equal-exposure dose gave +16% against +3%, so the study must be able to detect a gap of that size being removed. Second, four-core-genotype mice plus gonadectomy with and without hormone replacement, across rapamycin, acarbose and 17-alpha-estradiol, separating chromosomal sex from hormonal environment. Measure more than one endpoint in the same animals - survival, bone and motor function - because they do not point the same way.

2026-10-10 (re-audit): CORRECTION to the premise of this card. What_Changed asserted that the pharmacokinetic explanation 'was never a tested claim' and was 'one speculative line in a discussion'. That is wrong. Miller 2014 measured whole-blood rapamycin by HPLC-MS/MS in two separate cohorts (females 7/16/80 against males 6/9/23 ng/mL; sex p=0.007, interaction p=0.03), so the exposure difference is an established measurement. Only the causal step - whether equalising exposure removes the lifespan gap - is untested. The abstract's hedged 'perhaps reflecting sexual dimorphism in blood levels' refers to the causal inference, not to the measurement, and the card had conflated the two. The beginner text already stated the exposure difference as fact, so the two registers had been contradicting each other. Added in the same pass: the near-equal-exposure observation at 4.7 ppm (+16% female against +3% male), which argues against a purely pharmacokinetic account more directly than anything the card previously carried, and a note that MIL2014's exposure measurements come from animals separate from the survival cohort.
